newsitem.title: USA: U.S. 1997 oil demand to rise 1.3 pct from 1996-EIA.
newsitem.headline: U.S. 1997 oil demand to rise 1.3 pct from 1996-EIA.

text.p: U.S. petroleum demand in 1997 is expected to rise 1.3 percent from last year to 18.48 million barrels per day, the Energy Information Administration said Monday, hiking a previous forecast of no growth in 1997.

The higher demand outlook led EIA to revise up its projection for net imports of crude oil and products to 8.9 million bpd, from 8.84 million bpd in its previous forecast and from 8.42 million bpd in 1996.
However, net crude oil imports are expected to average 7.69 million bpd, down 10,000 bpd from EIA's previous projection, but up from 7.37 million bpd last year.
EIA continued to lower its price outlook for 1997, pegging imported crude oil at $19.15 per barrel, down from $20.00 in its earlier forecast, and down from $20.59 last year.

The price projections stayed on a downward course because "unusually warm weather" in January through April dampened heating demand, and renewed Iraqi oil exports and "gains in world production offset growth in world demand," EIA said in its quarterly short-term energy outlook.

U.S. crude production is expected to slip to 6.37 million bpd in 1997, down from 6.47 million bpd last year, but up 40,000 bpd from EIA's previous forecast with the help of new production in the Gulf of Mexico.
U.S. gasoline demand is seen rising 1.9 percent from last year to 8.00 million bpd, compared with a previous forecast of a 1.5 percent increase.

EIA hiked its projections for jet fuel and distillate by 10,000 bpd each to 1.62 million bpd and 3.41 million bpd respectively, pegging jet fuel demand growth at 2.5 percent from last year and distillate demand growth at 1.2 percent.
Demand for residual fuel is now expected to reach 850,000 bpd, up 40,000 bpd from EIA's previous forecast and up 1.0 percent from 1996.

"Electric utilities' demand (for residual fuel) is expected to recover somewhat from the depressed levels of the last two years, but this reflects, in part, a loss of nuclear power availability," EIA said.
The outlook assumed that U.S. Gross Domestic Product would grow by 3.7 percent in 1997.
